**Short answer:** An agreement made without consideration is generally void, unless it meets specific criteria such as being in writing and registered due to natural love and affection, or being a promise to compensate for something done, or being a promise to pay a debt barred by limitation law [S1][S6][S8].

**What the sources say:**

- An agreement without consideration is void, unless it is a promise to compensate, wholly or in part, a person who has already voluntarily done something for the promisor, or something which the promisor was legally compellable to do [S1][S6].
- An agreement without consideration is also void unless it is a promise, made in writing and signed by the person to be charged therewith, or by his agent generally or specially authorized in that behalf, to pay wholly or in part a debt of which the creditor might have enforced payment but for the law for the limitation of suits [S1][S6].
- In any of the cases where the agreement is made without consideration but meets the exceptions, "such an agreement is a contract" [S1][S6].

**What the sources say:**
* A temporary injunction may be granted if it is proved by affidavit or otherwise that "any property in dispute in a suit is in danger of being wasted, damaged or alienated by any party to the suit, or wrongfully sold in execution of a decree, or" [S1].
* A temporary injunction may also be granted if it is proved that "the defendant threatens, or intends, to remove or dispose of his property with a view to [defrauding] his creditors" [S1].
* Furthermore, a temporary injunction may be granted if "the defendant threatens to dispossess, the plaintiff or otherwise cause injury to the plaintiff in relation to any property in dispute in the suit" [S1].
* The court may grant such an order "to restrain such act, or make such other order for the purpose of staying and preventing the wasting, damaging, alienation, sale, removal or disposition of the property [or dispossession of the plaintiff, or otherwise causing injury to the plaintiff in relation to any property in dispute in the suit] as the Court thinks fit, until the disposal of the suit or until further orders" [S1].

**Short answer:** The market value of land is determined by the Collector using criteria such as the market value specified in the Indian Stamp Act, 1899, the average sale price of similar land in the nearest vicinity, or the consented compensation amount for certain projects, whichever is higher [S1].

**What the sources say:**
* The Collector must adopt criteria when assessing and determining the market value of the land, including:
    * "the market value, if any, specified in the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 (2 of 1899) for the registration of sale deeds or agreements to sell, as the case may be, in the area, where the land is situated" [S1].
    * "the average sale price for similar type of land situated in the nearest village or nearest vicinity area" [S1].
    * "consented amount of compensation as agreed upon under sub-section (2) of section 2 in case of acquisition of lands for private companies or for public private partnership projects, whichever is higher" [S1].
* The date for determining the market value must be "the date on which the notification has been issued under section 11" [S1].
* The average sale price is determined by considering sale deeds or agreements to sell for similar land in the near village or near vicinity area during the "immediately preceding three years of the year in which such acquisition of land is proposed to be made" [S1].
* When determining the market value, any price paid as compensation for land acquired earlier in the district "shall not be taken into consideration" [S1].
* Any price paid that the Collector believes "is not indicative of actual prevailing market value may be discounted for the purposes of calculating market value" [S2].
* If the market value cannot be determined due to restrictions on land transactions or lack of available sale deeds, the State Government can specify a "floor price or minimum price per unit area of the said land based on the price calculated in the manner specified in sub-section (1) in respect of similar types of land situated in the immediate adjoining areas" [S2].
* The Collector must take steps before starting land acquisition proceedings to "revise and update the market value of the land on the basis of the prevalent market rate in that area" [S3].
* The standard method for determining market value is by "evaluating the land on the date of publication of notification under Section 4(1) of the Act, acting as a hypothetical purchaser willing to purchase the land in open market at the prevailing price on that day, from a seller willing to sell such land at a reasonable price" [S8].
* The market value is determined with reference to the open market sale of comparable land in the neighborhood, by a willing seller to a willing buyer, on or before the date of preliminary notification, to give a fair indication of the market value [S8].
* The determination of market value depends on factors such as "the location of the land; area of the land; whether the land is in a developed area or not; whether the acquisition is of a small plot of land or a big chunk of land and number of other advantageous and disadvantageous factors" [S7].

**Uncertain or not covered:** The sources do not provide a comprehensive, step-by-step guide for all scenarios, nor do they detail the specific process for determining the "consented amount of compensation" mentioned in [S1].
